# Nano Banana 2.1 in Picsart: What It Does and 14 Prompts to Try

> **In short:** Google released Nano Banana 2.1 in October 2026, and it is now available inside Picsart's AI Playground. The new model generates and edits images from text or pictures, supports up to 4K output across 15 aspect ratios, and lets you refine a picture over a whole conversation.

A new image model just landed in a tool many people already use. If you've ever opened Picsart to make a quick poster, clean up a photo, or design a thumbnail, the engine under the hood just got an upgrade — and it's worth knowing what changed.

## What Nano Banana 2.1 actually does

Nano Banana is Google's family of image-generation models. According to Google's announcement, version 2.1 is now available in Picsart's AI Playground, which is the part of the app where you create and edit images with AI.

The new model works in two directions: it can generate an image from a text description, and it can edit an image you already have. You can also combine the two — start with a picture, describe a change, and watch it happen.

A few things stand out about this release:

- **Multiple output sizes.** The model produces images in 1K, 2K, or 4K (a measure of how many pixels the image contains — higher numbers mean a sharper, more detailed picture).
- **15 aspect ratios.** That's the shape of the image — square for Instagram, vertical for Stories, wide for YouTube, and so on.
- **Multi-turn editing.** You don't have to get your prompt perfect on the first try. You can refine the same picture over several messages, the way you'd ask a designer for tweaks.

## What the prompting guide suggests

Google also published a prompting guide alongside the release. A "prompt" is just the instruction you type to the AI. The guide groups 14 ready-to-copy prompts around the things Nano Banana 2.1 is reportedly best at. According to the guide, those strengths are:

- **Readable text on posters and diagrams.** Many image models still mangle words, so a model that handles text well is useful for flyers, slides, and social graphics.
- **Precise edits.** Small, controlled changes to an existing image — change a color, swap an object, fix a detail.
- **Doodle-directed changes.** You sketch a rough shape and tell the model what to do with it.
- **Combining several images.** Feed it a few reference pictures and ask for a scene that pulls them together.
- **Step-by-step refinement in one chat.** Build a picture across multiple messages instead of starting over each time.

The full list of 14 prompts lives in Google's prompting guide. The short version: each prompt is designed to test one of those strengths, so you can see for yourself what the model handles well.

## What this means for you

- **If you make things for fun or social media:** The text-on-images angle is the one to test first. A lot of AI art looks great until you ask for a word — then it turns into alphabet soup. If Nano Banana 2.1 actually keeps words readable, that saves you a trip to a separate text tool.
- **If you run a small business or work in marketing:** The combination of 4K output, 15 aspect ratios, and multi-turn editing is built for the messy reality of campaign work. One idea, many formats, and you can keep adjusting without re-uploading every time.
- **If you're a student or just learning:** Treat the 14 prompts as a mini tutorial. Copy one, change a few words, and see what changes in the output. That's the fastest way to learn how these models "think."
- **If you already use Picsart:** Open the AI Playground section of Picsart and look for the new Nano Banana 2.1 option. Start with one of the prompting-guide prompts, then try refining the result in a follow-up message — that's where multi-turn editing earns its keep.

## Wrap-up

Nano Banana 2.1 brings higher resolution, more shapes, and a more conversational editing flow to a tool a lot of people already have on their phone. The smartest first move is to pick one of the 14 prompts from Google's guide, paste it into Picsart's AI Playground, and see what comes back. From there, treat your second and third message as the real test — that's where the model shows whether it can take direction, not just produce a pretty first image.
